# freeze: auto is set project-wide in the root _quarto.yml.
# The run-benchmarks chunk below uses callr::rscript() to execute run_all.R
# safely from within knitr. Because of freeze: auto, benchmarks only re-run
# when explicitly requested:
#
#   Normal render (frozen, instant):     quarto render index.qmd
#   Re-run benchmarks + re-render:       quarto render index.qmd --no-freeze
---

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: run-benchmarks
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# BENCHMARK EXECUTION
#
# Runs the full benchmark suite via callr::rscript(), which is safe to call
# from within knitr. (system2("Rscript", ...) deadlocks on Windows because
# child processes inherit knitr's captured stdout/stderr connections.)
#
# freeze: auto (set project-wide in _quarto.yml) caches this chunk after the
# first successful render — subsequent renders skip it entirely.
#
# Workflow:
#   Normal render (use cached results):  quarto render index.qmd
#   Re-run benchmarks + re-render:       quarto render index.qmd --no-freeze
#
# stdout/stderr are captured to temp files so they survive knitr's output
# capture and print correctly on both success and failure.
#
# RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE stops renv from re-activating inside
# the callr subprocess. The parent knitr session already has the correct
# library loaded — renv re-activating in the child causes failures when the
# lockfile is out-of-sync, even if all needed packages are installed.
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

if (!requireNamespace("callr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Package 'callr' is required. Install with: install.packages('callr')")
}

# Capture stdout/stderr to temp files.
# callr's env argument REPLACES the subprocess environment when supplied,
# stripping PATH, R_HOME, etc. and causing Rscript.exe to fail before running
# a single line. Instead, set env vars in the PARENT session via Sys.setenv()
# so callr inherits the full environment unchanged.
stdout_file <- tempfile("run_all_stdout_")
stderr_file <- tempfile("run_all_stderr_")

# Restore env vars and remove temp files on chunk exit
old_renv_flag <- Sys.getenv("RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED", unset = NA)
old_iterations <- Sys.getenv("BENCHMARK_ITERATIONS", unset = NA)

on.exit({
  # Restore RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED
  if (is.na(old_renv_flag)) {
    Sys.unsetenv("RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED")
  } else {
    Sys.setenv(RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED = old_renv_flag)
  }
  # Restore BENCHMARK_ITERATIONS
  if (is.na(old_iterations)) {
    Sys.unsetenv("BENCHMARK_ITERATIONS")
  } else {
    Sys.setenv(BENCHMARK_ITERATIONS = old_iterations)
  }
  if (file.exists(stdout_file)) file.remove(stdout_file)
  if (file.exists(stderr_file)) file.remove(stderr_file)
}, add = TRUE)

# Set env vars in parent — callr subprocess inherits them automatically
Sys.setenv(
  RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED = "FALSE",  # Prevent renv re-activating in child
  BENCHMARK_ITERATIONS           = "1"
)

log_file <- "_results/run_all_log.txt"
if (!dir.exists("_results")) dir.create("_results", recursive = TRUE)

message("Running benchmark suite — output logged to: ", log_file)

result <- tryCatch({
  callr::rscript(
    script = "_scripts/run_all.R",
    wd     = getwd(),
    stdout = stdout_file,
    stderr = stderr_file
  )
  "success"
}, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))

# Always write full output to log file regardless of knitr capture
log_lines <- c(
  paste("=== run_all.R log:", Sys.time(), "==="),
  paste("Working directory:", getwd()),
  paste("Result:", result),
  "",
  "--- stdout ---",
  if (file.exists(stdout_file)) readLines(stdout_file, warn = FALSE) else "(empty)",
  "",
  "--- stderr ---",
  if (file.exists(stderr_file)) readLines(stderr_file, warn = FALSE) else "(empty)"
)
writeLines(log_lines, log_file)

if (result != "success") {
  stop(
    "run_all.R failed. Full output written to: ", log_file, "\n",
    "Open that file to see the actual error.\n",
    "callr: ", result
  )
}

message("Benchmark suite complete.")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: calc-sizes
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# CALCULATE FILE SIZES (fast — just stat() calls, runs at render time)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tools)

get_size_mb <- function(path) {
  if (file.exists(path)) file.size(path) / 1024 / 1024 else 0
}

get_shp_size_mb <- function(shp_path) {
  if (!file.exists(shp_path)) return(0)
  base_path <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(shp_path)
  exts <- c("shp", "shx", "dbf", "prj", "cpg")
  sidecars <- paste(base_path, exts, sep = ".")
  sum(file.size(sidecars[file.exists(sidecars)])) / 1024 / 1024
}

sizes <- tibble(
  Dataset = c("Addresses", "Addresses", "Counties", "Counties"),
  Format  = c("CSV", "Parquet", "Shapefile", "Parquet"),
  SizeMB  = c(
    get_size_mb("_data/utah_addresses.csv"),
    get_size_mb("_data/utah_addresses.parquet"),
    get_shp_size_mb("_data/utah_counties.shp"),
    get_size_mb("_data/utah_counties.parquet")
  )
)

if (!dir.exists("_results")) dir.create("_results")
write_csv(sizes, "_results/file_sizes.csv")
```

## The Challenge: Data Validation {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

::: {.incremental}
* **The Task**: We have **1.2 Million** address points in Utah.
* **The Goal**: Validate that the `CountyID` attribute matches the actual spatial location.
* **The Method**: Perform a **Point-in-Polygon** join against County Boundaries.
* **The Constraint**: Do it fast, reproducible, and (ideally) with low memory.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> "Is the address labeled 'Salt Lake County' actually *inside* the Salt Lake County polygon?"
:::

---

## The "Modern" Stack: Parquet

<div class="columns">
<div class="column" width="60%">
### What is it?
* **Columnar Storage**: Reads only the columns you need.
* **Typed Schema**: No more guessing if "049" is a string or number.
* **Compression**: Snappy/ZSTD compression reduces file size by ~60%.
* **GeoParquet**: Standardizes how geometry is stored (WKB) so any tool can read it.
</div>

<div class="column" width="40%">
![Parquet Structure](https://parquet.apache.org/images/parquet-layout.png){width="80%"}
</div>
</div>

---

## The "Modern" Stack: DuckDB

<div class="columns">
<div class="column" width="60%">
### What is it?
* **"SQLite for Analytics"**: An embedded SQL OLAP database.
* **Vectorized Engine**: Processes data in batches, not row-by-row.
* **Spatial Extension**: Adds geometry support (`ST_Within`, `ST_Intersects`).
* **Zero-Copy**: Queries Parquet files *directly* without importing data.
</div>

## Benchmark 02: Modern R (`DuckDB`) {.scrollable}

**The "Modern" Way**: Columnar Parquet + embedded SQL engine.

```{r}
#| file: _scripts/02_bench_duckdb.R
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note}
## DuckDB's SPATIAL_JOIN
DuckDB's spatial extension uses its own internal `SPATIAL_JOIN` operator for
`ST_Intersects` predicates — bypassing any explicit RTREE index. No `CREATE
INDEX` step is needed or helpful for spatial joins. DuckDB handles spatial
query planning automatically.
:::

---

## Benchmark 03: Legacy Python (`GeoPandas`) {.scrollable}

**The Python Standard**: Wraps `pandas` and `shapely`.

```{python}
#| file: _scripts/03_bench_geopandas.py
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Implicit Indexing
GeoPandas automatically builds an STRtree spatial index during `sjoin()`,
which makes it fast for in-memory spatial joins without explicit index
creation. For 29 non-overlapping county polygons, this implicit index is
highly efficient.
:::

## Benchmark 05: Modern R (`SedonaDB`) {.scrollable}

**The Arrow-Native Way**: DataFusion-backed spatial SQL, no JVM required.

```{r}
#| file: _scripts/05_bench_sedonadb.R
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How SedonaDB differs from DuckDB
Both are embedded single-node engines, but SedonaDB is built on Apache Arrow
+ DataFusion (Rust) with spatial as a first-class citizen from day one. There
is no explicit `CREATE INDEX` step — spatial indexing is managed internally
by the query planner. The R API is pipe-native: `sd_read_parquet() |>
sd_to_view() |> ...` rather than SQL DDL statements.

**Lazy evaluation**: `sd_read_parquet()` registers a view without scanning
any data — the actual Parquet read happens when `sd_collect()` executes the
query. This is why "Load Data" for SedonaDB is near-instant, and "Validation
(Join)" includes both scan and compute time.
:::

## Benchmark 06: Modern Python (`SedonaDB`) {.scrollable}

```{python}
#| file: _scripts/06_bench_sedonadb.py
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note}
## SedonaDB Python vs R
The Python and R SedonaDB packages share the same underlying Rust/DataFusion
engine. Performance should be nearly identical — any difference reflects Python
vs R interpreter overhead in the benchmark harness, not the engine itself.
Install: `conda install "apache-sedona[db]"`
:::

## Understanding the Results {background-color="#f0f0f0"}

### What the numbers actually show

::: {.incremental}
* **SedonaDB: 1.9s** — fastest overall, even though this includes the actual Parquet scan (lazy I/O)
* **GeoPandas: 3.1s** — fast because 29 polygons fit in RAM and implicit STRtree is efficient
* **sf: 28.6s** — pure in-memory but slow due to GEOS geometry overhead at 1.2M points
* **DuckDB: 50s (R) / 96s (Python)** — **slower than sf**, despite having an explicit RTREE index
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## DuckDB's SPATIAL_JOIN Bypasses Explicit RTREE Indexes
`EXPLAIN` confirmed: DuckDB's spatial extension intercepts any `ST_Intersects`
join and routes it through its own `SPATIAL_JOIN` + `SEQ_SCAN` operator,
ignoring user-created RTREE indexes entirely. The ~50s join time is DuckDB's
**actual** spatial join performance on this dataset — explicit indexes provide
no benefit. DuckDB's strength is analytical SQL, not optimized spatial joins.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## SedonaDB: Lazy Evaluation + Predicate Pushdown
SedonaDB's DataFusion engine reads only the Parquet data needed to satisfy the
join, applying spatial filters at scan time with no explicit index step. This is
why "Load Data" is ~0s (view registration only) and "Validation (Join)" at 1.9s
includes full I/O — yet still beats everything else.
:::
:::

---

## Why does this matter?

### 1. Scalability
* **Legacy**: Fails when Data > RAM.
* **Modern (DuckDB/SedonaDB)**: Streams data — processes datasets larger than RAM.

### 2. File Formats
* **Shapefile**: 3+ files (.shp, .shx, .dbf). Truncates column names. 2GB limit.
* **Parquet**: 1 file. Full column names and types. **79% smaller** (333MB CSV → 71MB Parquet).

### 3. Memory Efficiency
* **Legacy (sf/GeoPandas)**: 990MB–1.3GB resident for this dataset.
* **DuckDB**: 122MB load, ~2MB query — streams without holding all data in memory.
* **SedonaDB**: ~9MB — Rust arena + lazy scan reads only what the join needs.

### 4. Portability
* **SQL**: The join query in R was **identical** to the join query in Python.
* Logic lives in the *query*, not scattered across tool-specific APIs.

---

## Use Case Recommendations

| Scenario | Recommended Tool | Reason |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| **Small data (<100MB), one-off** | sf / GeoPandas | Simple, fast, no setup overhead |
| **Large data, repeated SQL queries** | DuckDB + Parquet | Index once, stream large datasets |
| **Large data, spatial joins** | SedonaDB + Parquet | Lazy pushdown, no explicit index needed |
| **Limited RAM** | DuckDB or SedonaDB | Both stream — legacy stack crashes |
| **Cross-language portability** | DuckDB + Parquet | Same SQL in R and Python |
| **Fastest spatial join, R** | SedonaDB | DataFusion outperforms explicit RTREE |

---

## Conclusion

| Feature | Legacy (sf/GeoPandas) | DuckDB | SedonaDB |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Format** | CSV / Shapefile | Parquet | Parquet |
| **Join Time** | 4–29s | ~33s (R) / ~58s (Python) | **1.5s** ✅ |
| **RAM Usage** | ~1–1.3 GB | ~120MB | ~9MB |
| **Index Setup** | Automatic | None (SPATIAL_JOIN handles it) | None needed |
| **Lazy I/O** | ✗ | ✗ | ✅ |
| **Language** | R / Python | R + Python | R |
| **Best For** | Small, one-off | Large SQL workflows | Fast spatial joins |

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-important}
## DuckDB's Explicit RTREE Has No Effect on Spatial Joins
`EXPLAIN` confirmed: DuckDB's `SPATIAL_JOIN` operator overrides user-created
RTREE indexes — both tables are scanned sequentially regardless. For spatial
joins, DuckDB's ~50s time is the real baseline. For large-scale non-spatial
SQL analytics and out-of-core processing, DuckDB remains the right tool.
:::
:::

### The winner for spatial joins: SedonaDB.
### The winner for portable, large-scale SQL: DuckDB.
